prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat moire bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: After the first round I keep B031 as my preferred configuration, with the same three names, and I want to say why in terms of mechanism and credit rather than counts. The Bistritzer-MacDonald result is a clean analytical statement: interlayer tunnelling renormalises the Dirac velocity, which vanishes at a discrete set of twist angles, and the largest of these (about 1 degree) gives bands that are flat to a degree that makes interactions dominant. That is a quantitative, falsifiable prediction from a transparent model, and it was made seven years before anyone could build the device. The 2018 experiments then found correlated insulating states and superconductivity at the predicted angle, and the tuning of interaction strength by twist and gate is something condensed-matter physics did not have before. Independent groups have since reproduced the correlated phases in devices of different construction, so the discovery does not rest on one laboratory. In my judgement this is a new regime of matter whose organising principle is understood at the single-particle level, which is what I mean by a discovery that is understood and not only observed. The decade since 2018 is enough time for the basic picture to be tested in many places. I have moved no further than that: the clock is a very strong alternative, and I would not oppose it, but I do not think the committee should choose it merely because its credit is easier to write.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 stand and some were sharpened by colleagues. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, so the citation must honour the flat-band prediction and the observation of the phases and must not imply an explanation. Credit is genuinely crowded: Cao and Fatemi (lead authors of the 2018 papers), Dean and the hBN-aligned work, the other early experimental groups, and the earlier continuum-model theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto all have claims that the three-name cap cannot meet. Bistritzer was a postdoc when the paper was written, and Olsson is right that the committee would have to explain the omissions clearly. Twist-angle disorder limits device-to-device reproducibility. Against B029 specifically, I concede that its credit is cleaner and that the precision and reproducibility are beyond dispute; my objection is that it refines a measurement programme already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and that is a judgement of weight, not of correctness.

responses.point: Olsson would not block B031 but would not make it her first choice yet, because the pairing mechanism is debated, device variability is large, and a three-name version requires a defensible explanation for omitting Cao and the early experimentalists.
responses.response: I accept most of this and it changes how I would word the citation, not the names. The mechanism and the variability are real, but neither concerns what is being credited: the prediction of the magic-angle flat bands and the observation of correlated phases at that angle. A citation that says exactly that carries no claim about the pairing. On Cao, I take the point seriously. The experimental credit in this configuration goes to the group leader whose programme found and led the field, and I think the committee has precedent for crediting the principal investigator and not the first-author student. I cannot claim the 2018 lead-author question is settled in my favour, and if the committee decided that three names cannot be defended I would rather drop Bistritzer than expand the list.

responses.point: Kroll presents the lattice clock as the cleanest measurement advance, with a two-name credit that is compact and defensible, and with real downstream reach in redshift tests, constants and the redefinition of the second, while naming the 2005 and 2012 prizes as his main reservation.
responses.response: On the evidence you cite I agree: independent clock comparisons at 1e-18 are exactly the kind of reproduction I trust, and the Katori-Ye pair is a fair reading of proposal and realisation. We disagree on how much weight the neighbouring prizes carry. You treat them as a sceptic's objection; I treat them as a real reason to prefer a result that opens a regime nobody had access to. I would also push on the chair's question about waiting for the redefinition of the second: if the citation rests on demonstrated performance, then that event is not required, and I would not hold B029 back for it. So my disagreement with you is a ranking judgement, and I will keep B029 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson supports the same B031 trio but cautions that earlier theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) found the twist-angle dependence of the bands, so the citation must not over-claim, and he names B016 as the better-matured alternative.
responses.response: I agree with the citation caution and have changed my wording to say prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene, which credits the quantitative magic-angle result without claiming the first observation that the bands depend on twist. On the chair's question to us both, I can only say with confidence that several independent groups, using different device constructions, have seen the correlated insulating states and superconductivity; I have not verified an exact count. I would treat the unresolved pairing mechanism as a footnote to the discovery and not a reason to defer, but I would not defend that if the committee's condensed-matter members disagree. On B016 I still think the attribution is the harder one, with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan, plus the death of Zhang.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes B029 plus B037 (Halzen alone for IceCube) as two distinct achievements within three names, and concedes that a sole credit for a large collaboration is exposed.
responses.response: I find the two-part idea reasonable in principle, but I would not support B037 as drafted. A single name for an observatory with an AMANDA precursor and many pioneers is, by your own account, the weak part, and the pairing of metrology with neutrino astronomy has no scientific link that I can see; it exists to fit the cap. The three-name limit is a constraint on the committee, not a reason to build a prize from two unrelated halves. For the same reason I prefer one coherent part with three names (B031) over two thin parts.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the flat-band prediction plus the observation of correlated phases as a prize-level discovery while the superconducting mechanism remains open.

Whether Bistritzer should be the third name, or whether a two-name pair (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero) is the more defensible configuration, and how the omission of Cao, Fatemi and Dean's group would be explained.
How many independent groups have reproduced superconductivity at the magic angle, and how robust it is across devices; I have not independently checked a count.
The exact priority history of the earlier twist-angle theory and of the early experimental groups, which I am recalling from memory.
Whether the committee, having heard the first round, prefers the cleaner two-name B029 and I am overweighting new regime of matter against a measurement advance.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any credited candidate. I have no known collaboration with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Katori or Ye. I share the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson, whose fields touch B004 and B001; I have weighed their statements on merit, and I note that Johansson has flagged possible recusal on B004, which does not affect my own configuration.
